intent.goal: Give people a fun, quickly playable TV-first 3D world that agents can expand and revise without the human managing the engine or build machinery.
invariants: A playable idea is more important than committing to a game engine.
The human can revise the same world later without losing a known-good version.
An optional external worker may improve fidelity but cannot be mandatory for every useful experience.

factors.question: How are world images produced?
factors.relevance: Rendering fidelity, TV hardware limits and agent iteration cost.

options.meaning: Android OpenGL ES/native renderer; requires device-specific testing.
WebGL/browser rendering; potentially easier to prototype, not proven on target TV.
A remote renderer streams frames; latency/network and expense matter.

factors.question: Where does game/world state advance?
factors.relevance: Authority over real-time gameplay, latency and offline behavior.

options.meaning: Local state updates and collision on the TV.
Remote state advancement with round-trip interaction.
Local predictions with asynchronous remote world simulation.

factors.question: What does the TV display as its direct interactive surface?
factors.relevance: A streamed scene and a local scene have different contracts.

options.meaning: TV displays locally constructed frames.
TV displays decoded frames received from elsewhere.

factors.question: What input experience is usable for real players?
factors.relevance: A D-pad cannot be assumed equivalent to full 3D camera control.

options.meaning: Minimal remote controls with navigation-friendly game design.
Game controller with continuous movement and camera control.
Second-screen gestures, virtual controls and semantic actions.

factors.question: How can scenes, models and animations evolve independently?
factors.relevance: Agent updates should not require replacing game execution for art changes.

options.meaning: Content is bundled with the current application artifact.
Data-only asset packs fetched on demand with hash checks and rollback.

factors.question: How do agents describe or update the world?
factors.relevance: Scene representation determines which small edits can be made independently.

options.meaning: Restricted declarative scene/behavior data with versioned semantics.
Engine-native scene and script project.
Agent-generated meshes and motions, independent of gameplay semantics.

factors.question: Which world identity and progress must survive updates?
factors.relevance: World ownership and user progress are separate from renderer or simulation.

options.meaning: Local durable world and player-state snapshots.
Versioned recoverable state shared across trusted devices.

factors.question: How is the next variant proposed and verified?
factors.relevance: Fast creative iteration without letting updates destroy the last playable candidate.

options.meaning: Git/CI produces a candidate implementation or verified asset.
Restricted scene change and immediate preview without rebuilding the engine.
A human selects and publishes versioned changes manually.

variants.purpose: Learn whether tiny 3D gameplay is fun and viable before choosing an engine.
Test local 3D rendering and independent asset updates against real Fire hardware.
Explore high-fidelity worlds with a remote GPU without treating the network path as solved.

intersections.reason: This proposed remote-rendering option delivers visual frames as a video stream.
The native rendering option owns local frame presentation.
Meaningful return to a remotely advanced world may require a recoverable shared state contract; investigate alternatives.
A constrained declarative world model might allow agent-designed D-pad-friendly control without heavy engine rewrites. This is not established.

experiments.question: Can a 3D object be controlled comfortably through the standard remote?
experiments.witness: Physical Fire TV D-pad trace, frame timing, and a human play impression.

experiments.question: Can an agent replace one 3D model without changing game rules or destroying the previous revision?
experiments.witness: Two immutable asset hashes, an actual renderer swap, a saved old build, and rollback on the TV.

experiments.question: Which network conditions make a streamed world noticeably worse than a locally simulated one?
experiments.witness: Measured input-to-photon latency under controlled network conditions, not synthetic guesses.
